description: Ramayana correspondences in 'The Dream of Ravan: A Mystery' (Dublin University Magazine serial 1853-54; 1895 Theosophical reprint, preface G.R.S.M.). The work retells Ramayana episodes as a Vedantic dream of Ravan — usually without citation; when it does cite, it cites other numberings (Adhyatma Ramayana Aranya-kanda V; Schlegel/Gorresio Adi-kanda XXIX/XXX).

target.numbering_notes: kanda/sarga in the Gita Press 1970s reprint numbering (= ramayana.info numbering); GP scans are the bindery archive.

sources.title: The Dream of Ravan: A Mystery
sources.publication: Dublin University Magazine 1853-54 (serial); reprint London: Theosophical Publishing Society, 1895, 262 pp.
sources.notes: anonymous; preface signed G.R.S.M. Locators are 1895-edition page anchors from the djvu.txt OCR (source_lines = same file's line numbers; OCR pages may lag the printed edition by the front matter).

entries.quote: Rama, the son of Dasha-ratha, King of Ayodhya, having been banished for fourteen years by his father to gratify the ambition of one of his younger queens, Kekaiyi, who wished
entries.episode: Editorial recap: Rama banished fourteen years by Dasharatha at Kekaiyi's urging (to secure succession for Bharata); wanders the wilds with Sita and Laxuman, slaying demons, goblins and giants

refs.notes: Kaikeyi's boons, the banishment decree and 14-year term (editorial recap; composite)

entries.notes: Opening editorial survey of the Ramayana; table block for the exile; decree/departure sargas not pinned. Kekaiyi=Kaikeyi; 'ioveliest' OCR slip for 'loveliest' (line 128) Editorial recap of the frame story only.

entries.quote: This lady had assigned for her maintenance the forest of Janasthana, covering an immense tract in the South of India, and lived here in considerable ease
entries.episode: Editorial recap: Shurpa-nakha ('Basket-nails', nails like winnowing baskets) dwells in Janasthana devouring Munis; falls in love with Rama's foot-print and tracks it
entries.notes: Backstory before the mutilation; foot-print-love detail is from the Adhyatma Ramayana, which the author cites at lines 218-221 ('[Aranya Kanda — Sarga V]'); patronymic note Raghava/Saumitri at 223-226 Editorial recap; Surpanakha's self-named 'winnowing-basket nails' motif belongs to her aranya 16 introduction.

entries.quote: Then, by the order of Rama, drawing his sword and seizing her, Laxuman, nimble mover, slit off her nose and ears.
entries.episode: Verse retelling: Shurpa-nakha propositions Rama, is fobbed off on Laxuman, threatens to devour Sita; Laxuman slits her nose and ears; she flees screaming to Khara
entries.source_citation_in_text: [Aranya Kanda — Sarga V] — but this is the Adhyatma Ramayana's Aranya-kanda numbering, not Valmiki's (vulgate Aranya-kanda sarga 5 is a different episode)
entries.notes: Headed 'The Unhappy Love of the Rakshasi... Translated from the Sanscrit'; author states source is the Adhyatma Ramayana [Aranya Kanda Sarga V]; events match Valmiki aranya 17-18; Laxuman=Lakshmana; footnote: Gautami=another name for Godavari Author cites the Adhyatma Ramayana's numbering while retelling Valmiki's episode — exactly the mis-sourced-paraphrase case HOL-263 targets.

entries.quote: And fourteen thousand Rakshasas, terrible in their deeds, He commanded to march upon Rama, thro' desire to effect his slaughter.
entries.episode: Verse retelling: Khara vows revenge and marches with 14,000 Rakshasas plus Trishiras and Dushana; Rama alone slays the whole host 'within half a watch'
entries.notes: Janasthana battle; footnote (460-461) glosses Khara='harsh', Trishiras='three heads', Dushana='crime'; Rama stations Laxuman with Sita in a cave first; OCR page anchor 37 lines below start

entries.quote: Brushing the bloody wounds of the weapons, she filled up the cavities by the volition of pure intention
entries.episode: Sita brushes/heals Rama's weapon-wounds after the battle; editorial footnote quotes the Sanskrit commentary and reads the 'brushing' as mesmeric traction
entries.notes: Sita healing Rama by 'volition of pure intention' (Satya-Sankalpatva) is an Adhyatma-Ramayana detail absent from Valmiki's Janasthana aftermath; author compares Du Potet's mesmeric rules

entries.quote: Lo! Khara lies slaughtered in battle; Trishiras, and Dushana too, And fourteen thousand other Rakshasas, all of them mighty in spirit, Have been in a moment by Rama slain
entries.episode: Verse retelling: Shurpa-nakha flees to Lanka, falls prostrate at Ravan's feet in council, reports the destruction of Khara's host and taunts him as king without spies
entries.notes: Report-to-Ravana scene follows the battle in the vulgate (table covers only to sarga 30); verse continues the Adhyatma text; OCR anchor 48 lines below start Inventory said aranya 30-31; corrected: the flight to Ravana's court is sarga 33 (30-31 is Akampana's report).

entries.quote: If I'm to be slain by the Spirit Supreme, I shall win the Vaikunta kingdom... I will, therefore, march against Rama.
entries.episode: Verse retelling: Ravan questions his sister (her speech re-narrates the mutilation and the battle); after a sleepless night he reflects that if slain by the Supreme Spirit he wins Vaikunta, and resolves to march against Rama
entries.notes: Death-at-Vishnu's-hands-as-liberation motive is an Adhyatma/Puranic overlay, not Valmiki's aranya narrative; includes the 'Panchavati.' scene-label at line 616 Corrected from aranya 31-32.

entries.quote: Thus all Ravan's subsequent violence and crime receives a religious colouring.
entries.episode: Editorial prose gloss: Ravan's hostile struggle with, and death at the hands of, Vishnu-incarnate read as his triumph — union with the Deity, a royal road quicker than devotion
entries.notes: Key interpretive crux of the whole book: the war as Ravan's chosen beatific catastrophe, drawn from the Vaikunta motive just narrated (dor-007); author calls it 'a necessary result from a pantheistic view'

entries.quote: after Indrajit, the heroic son of Ravan and Mandodari, has fallen to the bow of Laxuman, and several other leading chiefs of the Titanic army are killed, takes and burns Lanka, slays the ten-headed Titan, and recovers Sita
entries.episode: Editorial whole-story summary: Ravan carries off Sita (Mandodari scandalised); Rama with an army of talking monkeys under Hanumanta marches south, bridges the straits of Manaar, besieges Lanka; Indrajit falls to Laxuman's bow; Lanka taken and burned; ten-headed Titan slain; Sita recovered

refs.verified_against: ramayana.info sundara/53,54 (tail set fire; burning mansions)

entries.notes: Compressed retelling spanning the whole war; also implies bridge (yuddha 19-22); Mandodari 'weighty-stomach' pun; Hanumanta 'worshipped in India' with 'celebrated temple in Bombay'; Lanka 'perhaps the present Candy' (Kandy) Whole-story compression; 'takes and burns Lanka' = sundara 53-54 in GP numbering.

entries.quote: The first canto of the poem is, from this assembly, called the Sabha Parva, or “ Canto of the Assembly; ” and opens shortly after Indrajit is slain.
entries.episode: Editorial frame note: the poem opens on Ravan returning from a hard-fought day with Rama and Laxuman; he sleeps, dreams, wakes screaming, and summons his wise men; the Sabha Parva opens shortly after Indrajit is slain
entries.notes: Dates the frame's vantage to just after Indrajit's death; the dream-frame itself (Ravan sleeping and dreaming the story) is the author's invention, not a Valmiki scene

entries.quote: she will fondle and carry in her arms one cherished boy when he is snatched away; and will mourn her Indrajit a second time in the beloved Floribel.
entries.episode: Mandodari's consoled future destiny: in a later birth she will nurse Zingarel/Floribel's children and 'mourn her Indrajit a second time' in the beloved Floribel
entries.notes: Brief allusion to Indrajit's death woven into the Vedantic consolation of Mandodari (transmigration frame) The later-birth destiny is the author's own fantasy overlay, not Valmiki.

entries.quote: Nor for your sister, the long-nailed Shurpa-nakha, now slit both of nose and ears: nor for the dark-eyed Sulochana, the noble widow of our brave Indrajit!
entries.episode: Court scene: Mandodari's jealous interruption recalls Shurpa-nakha's mutilation and names Sulochana as Indrajit's widow; Sulochana's tribute — Sita 'the truest lady... most heroic wife... would that she were sent back with honour to her husband!'
entries.notes: Sulochana as Indrajit's named widow is post-Valmiki (later Puranic/vernacular) tradition; the bickering lady-rivals (Mahodari, Anunasika, Pankamagna, Ahankara, Gupta) are the author's comic inventions; 'sent back with honour' alludes to Sita's captivity and restoration

entries.quote: his own virtuous brother, Bibbishana, who, though most devotedly attached to his person and his government, never ceased to protest against his injustice in detaining Sita, and to warn him of the fatal results of persevering in such a course.
entries.episode: Vibhishana (Bibbishana) as loyal critic: protests against detaining Sita and warns Ravan of fatal results; origin of the 'Kamatur Rakshas' (love-sick Titan) nickname
entries.notes: Recasts Valmiki's pre-defection Vibhishana admonitions in Ravana's council (and his defection at 14-19) — here he stays devoted but critical; 'hallucination about Sita' ties nickname to the abduction

entries.quote: RAMAYANA — ADI — KANDA — SARGA XXIX, — ED. SCHLEGEL XXX. ED. GORRESIO. ... “ Here we are, most generous Raghava! Thy servants are we — command us. ”
entries.episode: Translated list of the Astras (supernatural weapons) delivered by Vishvamitra to Rama for his combat with the Titans, followed by the verse of their embodied appearance and Rama's command 'Dwell ye WITHIN MY MIND; and, being remembered, serve me'

refs.verified_against: ramayana.info bala/27 ('of those weapons'), bala/28 ('residing in my mind')

entries.source_citation_in_text: RAMAYANA — ADI-KANDA — SARGA XXIX ED. SCHLEGEL / XXX. ED. GORRESIO
entries.notes: Strongest explicit source citation in the book; catalogue 'constructed... from a comparison' of Schlegel and Gorresio editions (lines 4387-4390); vulgate number inferred as 28 from the table's bala 24-30 block (Tataka slain 26-27, Maricha struck 29-30); editorial frame reads astras as magic, mesmerism and electro-biology Strongest explicit citation in the book — but in 19th-century edition numbering, not GP numbering. GP/vulgate home of the astra grant + 'dwell within my mind' verse is bala 27-28 (content-verified).

entries.quote: If, assuming the shape of a golden deer, I am shot by an arrow from the bow of the divine Rama I shall attain instant emancipation; shall transcend for ever this sea of phenomenal illusion
entries.episode: Ravan recruits Maricha to assume the form of a beautiful deer and lure Rama and Lakshmana far from Sita's hermitage; Maricha, refusing at first, complies under threat — calculating that death by Rama's arrow means instant emancipation
entries.notes: Maricha recast as a timid ascetic Rishi master of siddhis; the moksha-by-Rama's-arrow motive is a Vedantic/Adhyatma-style overlay on Valmiki's terrified ogre (aranya 33-37 recruitment; the deer and his death-cry are aranya 42-45)

entries.quote: the auxiliary army of monkeys whom Sugriva, the king of Monkey-dom, and Hanuman, his prime minister, led on to the assistance of Rama.
entries.episode: Sugriva, king of Monkey-dom, and Hanuman, his prime minister, lead the monkey army to Rama's aid as the two armies encamp close by Lanka
entries.notes: Brief role-allusion within the siege frame (armies' outposts near each other, yuddha 28+); editorial bracket identifies the monkeys with the wild aboriginal hill-tribes of southern India (Bheels, Colis) won over by Rama

entries.quote: Thus Agni, or Fire, was his cook; Varuna, the Water Deity, his dhobi, or washerman; and this Vayu, or Wind, he made a sort of hamaul.
entries.episode: Ravan has subdued and enslaved all the elemental deities as domestic servants — Agni cook, Varuna washerman, Vayu sweeper/errand-runner who wheels his Vimana and pulls his punka
entries.notes: Draws on Ravana's conquest-of-the-gods backstory (uttara block per table); the comic domestication and the Vayu-as-messenger device (summoning Ananta Rishi) are the author's inventions

entries.quote: the hand of King Janaka's [adopted] daughter Sita, who was won by Rama from all competitors by his breaking the bow of Shiva, which none of the others could even bend
entries.episode: Ravan's failure in the contest for Sita's hand: Rama wins her from all competitors by breaking Shiva's bow, which none of the others could even bend
entries.notes: Sita swayamvara / bow-breaking within the table's bala 52-67 block; 'adopted' is bracketed editorially; Ravan-as-failed-suitor is a detail later vernacular tradition expands (Valmiki names Rama's rivals generically)

entries.quote: the straits separating the island of Lanka from the main land, across which Rama and the monkeys afterwards built Rama's bridge.
entries.episode: Rama and the monkeys afterwards built Rama's bridge across the straits to Lanka; antiquarian aside on 'Sita-Hrad' (Sita's Well) in the estuary and Sita found by Janaka in a furrow — thence 'Sita, or Furrow-found'
entries.notes: Bridge is a forward reference from the pre-war frame ('afterwards'); furrow-birth sits in the table's bala 52-67 block (Janaka's account); Sita-Hrad local tradition and the 'Sit' etymology are the author's antiquarian asides

entries.quote: when Sita was made a captive in the Ashoka grove, all presents, and all communications of a kind and courteous intent, were sent to her through Ghanta Patali
entries.episode: Sita held captive in the Ashoka grove; all kind presents and messages reach her through the child Ghanta Patali, whom Sita teaches embroidery, garland-stringing and song during 'the sad hours of her captivity'
entries.notes: Ashoka-vatika captivity (Sita found there sundara 14-16; captivity scenes run on); the child go-between Ghanta Patali is the author's invention — a Trijata-like kindness figure; her resemblance to Sita drives the frame plot
